# How a vaccine teaches your body to fight an infection

*Test fixture written for this repo.*

A vaccine trains your immune system to recognise a germ before you ever meet the real thing.

First, the vaccine shows the body a harmless piece or copy of the germ: a protein from its surface, a weakened version, or instructions that let your own cells make the protein for a short time.

Next, cells of the immune system find this unfamiliar protein and raise the alarm. Specialist cells called B cells start making antibodies, which stick to the protein and mark it for destruction. Other cells, called T cells, learn to find and destroy infected cells.

Then the body keeps a record. After the response settles down, some B and T cells stay on as memory cells, sometimes for years.

Finally, if the real germ arrives later, the memory cells recognise it at once. The body makes antibodies within days instead of weeks, often before you feel ill.

Many people think a vaccine works like a medicine that kills the germ. It doesn't: it works by training your own immune system, which is why it has to be given before an infection, and why some vaccines need boosters as memory fades.

Vaccines can cause short-lived side effects such as a sore arm or a mild fever. These are signs of the immune system learning, not of the infection itself.
